title: The forty tradition
hookLine: scholars gathered forty hadith, hoping for a reward promised in a report

cards: Here is a book that begins by admitting something.

In the introduction to his little collection of forty hadith, the scholar al-Nawawi mentions a report: whoever preserves forty hadith about the religion for the Prophet's community will be raised among the people of knowledge.
He says that promise is what moved scholars before him to gather forties of their own. And right there, in his own introduction, al-Nawawi says the report is weak.
Yesterday's question, sitting on the first pages of a real book. So why write it at all? Today: the forty tradition.

teach.h: THE HOPE IN A WEAK REPORT.
teach.b: The report promises that someone who preserves forty hadith for the community, on matters of the religion, will be raised with the scholars.
Al-Nawawi notes that it comes by many routes and that the hadith critics agree it is weak.
He also names scholars before him who gathered forties anyway, on belief, on law, on renouncing the world, on good manners, each with a different aim. But he doesn't rest his book on the weak report.

He points instead to sound ones: the Prophet's instruction that whoever is present should pass his words on to whoever is absent, and the prayer for the one who hears his words and conveys them as he heard them.
That's the prayer from the day on memorizing chains, now holding up a whole book. Next, what he gathered.
Not forty on a single subject, but sayings he considered foundations, each one, as he described it, a great principle of the religion.
His collection opens with the report on intentions, the line that also opens Bukhari's Sahih. The second is the hadith of Jibril: Islam, iman and ihsan.
And religion is sincere counsel, memorized two days back, has its place too. Last, why forty. The book never claims the number is holy.

teach.h: A BOOK THAT FITS IN A MEMORY.
teach.b: It's a number a person can carry: a book built to fit inside a memory, learned, recited, taught line by line, small enough to take anywhere and deep enough to keep opening.

how: Muslim students learn and memorize al-Nawawi's forty, line by line with a teacher, and other scholars have compiled forties of their own on many subjects.

games.q: the forty tradition — tap the pairs.

s: al-Nawawi calls the forty-hadith report sound
in his own introduction he says the critics agree it is weak, and he rests his book on sound reports.
al-Nawawi's collection opens with the hadith on intentions
actions are only by intentions comes first; the hadith of Jibril comes second.
every forty collection is about a single topic
al-Nawawi names forties on belief, law, renouncing the world and manners. his own gathers foundations.

games.q: you're al-Nawawi. the report that inspired forty-hadith collections is weak. what do you do?
o: drop the whole idea of a forty.
write the forty, say plainly the report is weak, and rest the book on sound reports.
call the report sound, so no one doubts the book.
games.why: he writes it, names the weakness himself, and grounds his work on sound reports about passing the Prophet's words on.

practice: Take the collection's first two sayings, both met on this path: actions are only by intentions, then Islam, iman, ihsan. Say them in order, one on each slow breath.
Then let a question rest, without a quick answer: if you could carry forty sayings anywhere, which would you want in your pocket first?

wordCard.voice: The forty tradition. Collections of forty hadith, gathered in hope of a promise from a weak report, and grounded by al-Nawawi on sound reports about passing the Prophet's words on. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the forty, the name given to this kind of collection.
